questions.q: What is a poison-pill message, according to this lesson?
options: A message that fails processing no matter how many times it's retried
Any message that arrives out of order
A message with a valid schema that always processes successfully
A message produced with acks=all
questions.explain: Unlike a transient failure, a poison pill fails no matter how many retries it gets — the message itself is the problem.

questions.q: Why does retrying a poison-pill message forever actually make things worse on a Kafka partition?
options: Kafka guarantees order within a partition and won't skip ahead, so the retry blocks every event behind that message on the same partition
It causes the broker to delete the entire topic
It has no negative effect at all, since Kafka processes partitions in parallel automatically
It converts the message into a valid one after enough retries
questions.explain: Because order within a partition is guaranteed, a consumer stuck retrying one message can't move on to the next one — everything behind it on that partition waits.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a bounded retry with backoff for a transient failure, instead of immediately sending it to a dead-letter topic?
options: A transient failure, like a downstream timeout, usually succeeds if the same message is simply retried a moment later — sending it straight to a DLQ would throw away a perfectly good message
Retries are never useful in a streaming pipeline
Backoff removes the need for a dead-letter topic entirely
A transient failure is exactly the same thing as a poison pill
questions.explain: Treating every failure like a poison pill wastes messages that would have succeeded on a simple retry — bounded retries with backoff catch that case first.

questions.q: Why does idempotent processing (Career & Capstone Lesson 11) matter for both retries and dead-letter handling, per this lesson?
options: A message can end up processed more than once in both patterns, so processing has to produce the same result whether it happens once or twice
Idempotency is only relevant to producers, never to consumers
Retries and dead-letter handling make idempotency completely unnecessary
Idempotent processing means a message is never processed more than once, so this concern is irrelevant
questions.explain: A crash between processing and committing, or a retry whose confirmation was lost, can both cause reprocessing — idempotent logic (like an UPSERT instead of a blind INSERT) is what keeps that safe.

questions.q: In this lesson's dead-letter code, why does the consumer still call consumer.commit(msg) after routing a failed message to orders-dlq?
options: So the consumer group's offset advances past the poison-pill message, letting the partition keep moving instead of getting stuck reprocessing it forever
Committing after a failure is a mistake and should never be done
It has no effect — commit only matters on a successful process_order() call
It deletes the message from the dead-letter topic
questions.explain: Once the message is safely routed to the DLQ, committing its offset lets the consumer move past it instead of retrying the same poison pill indefinitely.
